video_title: Psychiatry, Insane Asylums, Mental Illness, ECT, Lobotomies, Freud & Jung | Lex Fridman Podcast #502
gist: Historian of psychiatry Andrew Scull argues to Lex Fridman that psychiatry is in crisis on three fronts at once: a DSM diagnostic system built for reliability rather than validity that leading NIMH directors themselves denounced, a roughly $20 billion bet on genetics and neuroscience that Thomas Insel conceded improved patients' lot 'not one bit,' and a drug arsenal that is no real advance on the accidental discoveries of the 1950s. He traces a repeating historical pattern in which desperate remedies (Henry Cotton's organ removals, malaria therapy, insulin coma, lobotomy, unmodified ECT) each claimed roughly 80% cure rates, won Nobel Prizes, and died from generational turnover or a rival technology rather than from evidence, and warns that ketamine and psychedelics are being hyped as miracle depression cures on enormously weak evidence.

insights.claim: The DSM-III task force led by Robert Spitzer in 1980 deliberately built psychiatric diagnosis as a symptom-checklist system optimized for reliability (two clinicians reaching the same label) rather than validity (the label matching an underlying reality), and that same architecture still underpins diagnosis today.
insights.speaker: Andrew Scull
insights.so_what: Every downstream commercial structure built on DSM categories - drug indications, insurance reimbursement codes, clinical trial endpoints - rests on a classification its own architects only claimed was consistent, not true.
insights.quote: That didn't mean necessarily it was a valid diagnostic system

insights.claim: DSM-5 was launched in the early 2000s with the explicit goal of rebasing diagnosis on underlying pathology using the decoded human genome and neurotransmission research, but by about 2008 its authors gave up and fell back on the 1980 symptom-based approach.
insights.speaker: Andrew Scull
insights.so_what: A decade of genomics and neuroscience investment failed to produce a single biologically grounded psychiatric diagnosis, a cautionary base rate for anyone underwriting precision-psychiatry claims.

insights.claim: When DSM-5 was published, Thomas Insel and Steven Hyman - the then-current and preceding directors of the National Institute of Mental Health - publicly denounced it as unscientific and useless, while DSM-III's Robert Spitzer and DSM-IV's Allen Frances attacked it for being produced in secrecy.
insights.speaker: Andrew Scull
insights.so_what: The field's own institutional leadership has disowned the manual that still governs reimbursement and regulatory approval, a legitimacy gap that eventually forces revision of what counts as a treatable indication.
insights.quote: denounced the document as unscientific and useless

insights.claim: Psychiatric genetics has undermined rather than confirmed the DSM categories: roughly three hundred small genome variations account for only about ten percent of schizophrenia, and the genetic abnormalities raising susceptibility to bipolar disorder, schizophrenia and autism overlap heavily.
insights.speaker: Andrew Scull
insights.so_what: If the diagnostic boxes are not genetically distinct entities, drug development targeting them by label is aiming at constructs rather than diseases, which helps explain repeated late-stage CNS trial failures.
insights.quote: if we use three hundred small variations in the genome, we can account for about ten percent of schizophrenia

insights.claim: Some leading psychiatrists are speculating that within ten years the field will have to concede there is no such thing as schizophrenia or bipolar disorder as discrete illnesses, and Scull expects that admission to further damage public trust in psychiatry even though it is where the science points.
insights.speaker: Andrew Scull
insights.so_what: A category collapse of this scale would reset clinical trial design, diagnostic coding and the entire marketing architecture of psychiatric drugs within a decade.
insights.quote: there's no such thing as schizophrenia, there's no such thing as bipolar disorder

insights.claim: Scull describes 'diagnostic creep' as a recurring mechanism in which a core of unambiguous severe cases expands into a surrounding penumbra, and cites DSM-IV chief editor Allen Frances's conviction that the huge rise in autism diagnoses came more from Frances loosening the criteria than from more actual cases.
insights.speaker: Andrew Scull
insights.so_what: Diagnosed prevalence growth in psychiatric conditions can be a criteria artifact rather than a real epidemiological trend, which inflates addressable-market estimates built on diagnosis counts.
insights.quote: the huge increase in the number of diagnoses of autism is more driven by the fact he loosened the criteria for the diagnosis

insights.claim: Thomas Insel, after running NIMH for about thirteen years and funding an enormous volume of genetics and neuroscience research, conceded that roughly $20 billion of spending left the lot of the mentally ill improved not one bit.
insights.speaker: Andrew Scull
insights.so_what: The single largest public research bet in mental health produced no measurable patient benefit, the clearest available prior on expected returns from brain-disease-first approaches to mental illness.
insights.quote: after spending 20 billion dollars, the lot of the mentally ill has improved not one bit right?

insights.claim: Scull characterizes the field's half-century swing with Leon Eisenberg's line that psychiatry moved from brainless to mindless, meaning the enthusiasm for neuroscience discarded psychological and social insight just as the Freudians had earlier discarded biology.
insights.speaker: Andrew Scull
insights.so_what: A field that oscillates between total explanatory models rather than integrating them will keep producing decade-long research fashions that end in disappointment.
insights.quote: When I entered psychiatry, it was brainless psychiatry, leaving it mindless psychiatry.

insights.claim: Everything psychiatry currently offers is symptomatic treatment rather than cure, with no equivalent of penicillin for any psychiatric condition, and treatments themselves generate iatrogenic harm - Scull cites PTSD exposure therapy making a significant share of patients worse.
insights.speaker: Andrew Scull
insights.so_what: Framing psychiatric products as symptom management with a real harm tail, rather than as cures, is the honest base case for both clinical expectations and liability exposure.
insights.quote: We don't have a psychiatric penicillin for any of the conditions we're gonna be talking about

insights.claim: Neuroscience failed to throw up new drug targets, so pharmaceutical companies concluded they could make more money researching other diseases and abandoned mental illness, leaving a drug set that Steven Hyman says is no real advance on the compounds found by accident in the 1950s.
insights.speaker: Andrew Scull
insights.so_what: Major pharma has structurally exited psychiatric drug discovery, leaving new development to small startups - which concentrates both the opportunity and the risk in early-stage CNS biotech.

insights.claim: Despite cataloguing psychiatry's biological failures, Scull says he would be astonished if the major forms of mental illness did not have a biological component, and calls the absence of research by the players with the most money to develop better treatments depressing.
insights.speaker: Andrew Scull
insights.so_what: The critic's own position is that the biological pipeline is underfunded rather than misguided, which argues the pharma retreat is a capital-allocation failure rather than a verdict on the science.
insights.quote: the fact that there's no research being done by the people with the most money to develop better treatments is well, one word for it would be depressing

insights.claim: Scull identifies a recurring 80 percent cure claim as the signature of therapeutic overreach in psychiatry, appearing in the early asylums, in Henry Cotton's surgical work and in insulin coma therapy alike, and explicitly maps that pattern onto present-day breakthrough rhetoric.
insights.speaker: Andrew Scull
insights.so_what: A reusable screening heuristic: implausibly round, high cure rates in a field with no biomarker are a historical marker of claims that will not survive controlled trials.
insights.quote: 80% cure for Cotton's work, 80% cure for insulin coma therapy, 80% cure for the early asylums. This is overblown rhetoric

insights.claim: Henry Cotton, head of the New Jersey State Mental Hospital at Trenton from 1916, treated madness as focal sepsis and progressively pulled teeth, removed tonsils, stomachs, spleens and colons while claiming to cure eighty percent of patients, even though 45 percent of those given abdominal surgery died within a year.
insights.speaker: Andrew Scull
insights.so_what: An institution can sustain a treatment with a near-50 percent one-year mortality for decades when outcome measurement is controlled by the practitioner.
insights.quote: Stomachs are like cement mixers on a construction site and could be dispensed with.

insights.claim: Cotton's work was validated by the highest-status gatekeepers of its day - a prestigious Princeton lecture series, publication by Oxford and Princeton University Presses, and a New York Times write-up hailing it as a great breakthrough - and his successors continued pulling teeth and tonsils until 1960.
insights.speaker: Andrew Scull
insights.so_what: Elite institutional endorsement is not an independent check on therapeutic claims; it can be the mechanism that entrenches them for forty years.

insights.claim: Two of psychiatry's only Nobel Prizes went to interventions later discredited: Wagner-Jauregg's 1937 award for infecting general paralysis of the insane patients with malaria, and Egas Moniz's 1949 medicine prize for lobotomy, awarded just fourteen years after the procedure was invented.
insights.speaker: Andrew Scull
insights.so_what: The field's top external validation signal has a documented false-positive rate on exactly the kind of dramatic intervention it is asked to adjudicate.
insights.quote: Moniz wins the Nobel Prize in medicine in 1949 for lobotomy

insights.claim: Insulin coma therapy for schizophrenia, claimed by Sakel to cure eighty percent of patients, required a course of up to sixty comas, carried a one to five percent mortality rate and caused brain damage and obesity, and survived from 1933 until a randomized controlled trial in the 1950s failed it.
insights.speaker: Andrew Scull
insights.so_what: The controlled trial, not accumulating clinical experience, was the only thing that terminated a two-decade treatment - the decisive argument for demanding trial evidence before scale-up.
insights.quote: It turned out to have a mortality rate of one to five percent

insights.claim: Lobotomy ended not through evidence but through generational turnover plus the arrival of a rival technology, as younger psychiatrists who saw the incontinent back-ward casualties rebelled and had antipsychotic drugs available that looked more like regular medicine.
insights.speaker: Andrew Scull
insights.so_what: Discredited practices in medicine are displaced by substitutes and cohort replacement rather than refuted by data, which sets the realistic timeline for any entrenched standard of care being unseated.
insights.quote: I could teach any damn fool to perform a lobotomy in twenty minutes even a psychiatrist.

insights.claim: Asylums founded on the promise of curing 60 to 80 percent of patients were actually discharging only 35 to 40 percent, so each year left behind a residue of chronic patients until the accumulated chronic population came to define the institution's public image.
insights.speaker: Andrew Scull
insights.so_what: A stock-versus-flow accounting error - measuring cures against annual admissions while chronic cases accumulate - can make a genuinely partially effective institution look like a total failure.
insights.quote: They were discharging 35 or 40% of their patients

insights.claim: When asylum cure rates were exposed as nearer 10 to 12 percent, the profession blamed the patients by adopting degeneration theory - casting them as evolutionary throwbacks with defective brains - which converted the asylum from a therapeutic project into a custodial one.
insights.speaker: Andrew Scull
insights.so_what: When a professional promise fails publicly, redefining the population as untreatable is a cheaper institutional response than admitting the method failed, and it licenses far worse policy.

insights.claim: California pioneered forced sterilization of mental patients and continued the practice until about 1960, with over 60,000 sterilizations performed in the US by the 1960s and California accounting for a disproportionate share.
insights.speaker: Lex Fridman
insights.so_what: Coercive population policy ran inside a modern democratic state for roughly four decades, a reminder of how long institutional practice can outlive the discredited theory that justified it.
insights.quote: over 60,000 sterilizations have been performed in the US

insights.claim: The Rockefeller Foundation chose psychiatry as its priority investment area around 1930, partly because several trustees had mental illness in their own families, and among the geneticists it funded was Ernst Rudin in Germany, who became a leading proponent of sterilization and then of murdering mental patients.
insights.speaker: Andrew Scull
insights.so_what: Concentrated private philanthropy in a field with weak science can export an ideology as effectively as it funds research, a governance risk wherever one funder dominates a nascent discipline.

insights.claim: The mentally ill were the first victims of the Final Solution through Hitler's T4 program, which killed as many as a quarter million people and was where the gas chamber and the technique of disguising it as showers were developed, and German psychiatry for the most part collaborated.
insights.speaker: Andrew Scull
insights.so_what: The professional class closest to the patients supplied the rationale and the personnel, which is why Scull treats internal professional dissent as an insufficient safeguard compared with external checks and balances.
insights.quote: which may have been as many as a quarter million people, that the technology of the gas chamber was developed

insights.claim: In mental hospitals through the 1940s, 50s and 60s, ECT was overwhelmingly deployed as a punitive instrument of behavioral discipline and control rather than as a therapeutic intervention, with patients moderating their own behavior to avoid repeat treatments.
insights.speaker: Andrew Scull
insights.so_what: The historical case against ECT is really a case against institutional incentives, which is why modern evidence about the procedure and public sentiment about it have diverged so sharply.
insights.quote: ECT was much more used as a device to control people's behavior, than as a therapeutic intervention

insights.claim: Introducing muscle relaxants and anesthesia eliminated the spinal and hip fractures of unmodified ECT but made it a more complicated procedure requiring anesthesiologists and breathing support, while memory loss remains a widely recognized and disputed price of treatment.
insights.speaker: Andrew Scull
insights.so_what: The modification that made ECT safe also made it capital and staff intensive, which constrains supply independently of clinical demand.

insights.claim: Scull concedes that recent controlled trials provide decent evidence that ECT works for some severely distressed and suicidal depression patients, while stressing that it is a purely empirical treatment with no understood mechanism and typically requires repeat maintenance sessions rather than curing anything.
insights.speaker: Andrew Scull
insights.so_what: A treatment can be evidence-backed and mechanistically opaque at the same time; the opacity, not the evidence, is what keeps adoption and reimbursement suppressed.

insights.claim: The film of One Flew Over the Cuckoo's Nest fixed public opposition to ECT for decades and still creates hesitation today, and in California ECT now almost cannot be given to involuntarily confined patients because consent is required - an unusual legal constraint for a medical procedure.
insights.speaker: Andrew Scull
entities: One Flew Over the Cuckoo's Nest
insights.so_what: A single cultural artifact produced durable regulatory and utilization effects on a medical technology, the clearest case in the conversation of narrative risk outweighing clinical data.

insights.claim: Treatment-resistant depression is defined purely by failure to respond to drugs rather than by any distinct underlying disease, which Scull flags as a conceptually revealing label.
insights.speaker: Andrew Scull
insights.so_what: An entire commercial category is defined by the failure of the incumbent product class rather than by biology, so its size is a function of how poorly existing drugs work.

insights.claim: Psychoanalysis originated with Breuer's patient Anna O. (Bertha von Pappenheim) and the notion that repressed memories resurface as physical and psychological symptoms, and Freud replaced hypnosis with free association only after concluding he was a clumsy hypnotist and learning that Charcot's hypnotized hysterics in Paris had been performing rehearsed routines.
insights.speaker: Andrew Scull
insights.so_what: The founding evidence base of the twentieth century's dominant therapeutic paradigm was a handful of case vignettes built on a technique its originator had already found to be partly theatrical.

insights.claim: Freud's 1909 Clark University lectures, retrospectively framed as a Freud conference, were actually an afterthought at a thirty-speaker event that included two Nobel physics laureates and Franz Boas, and mainstream American psychiatry dismissed talk therapy for what it regarded as a biological condition.
insights.speaker: Andrew Scull
insights.so_what: In-house histories systematically inflate the founding moment of a paradigm, so origin stories told by a field about itself deserve the same discount as management's account of its own track record.

insights.claim: Freud himself lamented that his case histories read like short stories and therefore lacked the stamp of serious science, which Scull argues is precisely why novelists, playwrights, screenwriters and surrealists embraced psychoanalysis while clinical psychiatry did not.
insights.speaker: Andrew Scull
insights.so_what: Cultural adoption and scientific validation are separate distribution channels, and a theory can dominate the first for fifty years while failing the second.
insights.quote: my case histories read like short stories

insights.claim: Jung, not Freud, captured the wealthiest American patrons - a McCormick heir to the International Harvester fortune, Edith Rockefeller McCormick who wrote him big checks, and Paul and Mary Mellon whose foundation subsidized Princeton University Press publishing his works - and Scull suggests that patronage gap probably exacerbated the 1913 Freud-Jung split.
insights.speaker: Andrew Scull
insights.so_what: Patron capital shaped which branch of psychoanalysis got published and institutionalized, an early example of funding determining which intellectual franchise survives.

insights.claim: Psychoanalysis could never scale: circa 1930 roughly three hundred analysts in North America each seeing patients five hours a week could treat only a few thousand people while hundreds of thousands sat in mental hospitals, and its training institutes sat outside the universities just as universities were becoming the post-war knowledge factories.
insights.speaker: Andrew Scull
insights.so_what: A service model with fixed practitioner throughput and training controlled outside the dominant distribution platform loses to a scalable substitute regardless of its intellectual merits.
insights.quote: circa 1930 there are probably three hundred psychoanalysts in North America

insights.claim: Rockefeller Foundation funders Alan Gregg and Robert Morison repeatedly pressed analysts for proof their treatment worked and were refused on the grounds that reconstructing entire personalities cannot be measured, while clinical psychologists built training that included two years of scientific research methods and consequently knew how to win federal grants that the analysts could not obtain.
insights.speaker: Andrew Scull
insights.so_what: Refusing to be measured cost psychoanalysis the funding pipeline and with it the field - the clearest historical case that measurability, not efficacy, decided which therapy won.

insights.claim: CBT displaced psychoanalysis because its techniques could be packaged, reproduced, tested and delivered short-term rather than over five hours a week for years, yet Cochrane Reviews rate the evidence for CBT only low-to-medium confidence and the evidence in schizophrenia is poor.
insights.speaker: Andrew Scull
insights.so_what: The winning therapy won on packaging and testability rather than demonstrated superiority, which means the incumbent standard of care is itself vulnerable to a better-measured challenger.
insights.quote: the evidence for CBT is of low and medium confidence

insights.claim: Chlorpromazine, the compound that launched modern psychopharmacology, was an 1880s antihistamine that Rhone-Poulenc handed out to see if it might work as an antiemetic, an eczema treatment or an anesthetic potentiator, and only became a psychiatric drug because naval surgeon Henri Laborit noticed his pre-surgical patients stopped caring and wrote that it worked like a chemical lobotomy.
insights.speaker: Andrew Scull
insights.so_what: The foundational asset of an entire drug class was found by unplanned repurposing in an era with no trial controls, not by targeted discovery.
insights.quote: this works like a chemical lobotomy

insights.claim: The first two American drug companies approached to license chlorpromazine declined on the view there was no market, but SmithKline & French bought it and within two years two million people were taking the drug, transforming the firm from a small operator into a big company.
insights.speaker: Andrew Scull
insights.so_what: The largest psychiatric franchise of the century was twice passed over by incumbents who misjudged the market, and the buyer's advantage came from sales execution rather than science.
insights.quote: within two years, two million people are taking this drug

insights.claim: SmithKline & French created demand by putting its best salesmen on state legislatures and politicians with moving pictures of agitated patients turning calm, precisely because hospital psychiatrists were not yet interested in the idea of a chemical treatment.
insights.speaker: Andrew Scull
insights.so_what: Where the clinical customer is unconvinced, the budget holder can be sold instead - the original template for pharmaceutical policy marketing that still shapes psychiatric drug adoption.

insights.claim: Major tranquilizers were renamed antipsychotics in the early 1960s, implying they attacked the underlying psychosis, but they only dampen the positive symptoms of hallucination and delusion for a subset of patients and do little or nothing for the negative symptoms of apathy, language poverty and lost social capacity.
insights.speaker: Andrew Scull
insights.so_what: A category rename did the work of a mechanism claim, and the untreated negative symptoms remain the largest unmet need and the real target for any genuine breakthrough.

insights.claim: The 2005 NIMH-funded CATIE study published in the New England Journal of Medicine found that the newer patented second-generation antipsychotics, up to ten times more expensive than the off-patent first-generation drug, were not more efficacious, and that between 67 and 82 percent of patients dropped out of the trial depending on the drug.
insights.speaker: Andrew Scull
insights.so_what: An independent head-to-head trial destroyed the premium pricing rationale for a whole drug generation, the strongest argument in the episode for funding non-industry comparative trials.
insights.quote: Between 67% and 82% of the patients, depending on which drug they were on, dropped out of the trial

insights.claim: Second-generation antipsychotics traded one iatrogenic harm for another, reducing tardive dyskinesia somewhat while causing weight gain of 10 to 50 pounds that brings metabolic syndrome, diabetes and heart trouble.
insights.speaker: Andrew Scull
insights.so_what: Side-effect substitution rather than elimination means the long-run cost burden of the newer drugs shifts to cardiometabolic care rather than disappearing.

insights.claim: SSRIs beat placebo by a statistically significant but not clinically significant margin - improvement of one or two points on a 60-point rating scale can clear statistical significance - while over forty percent of depressed patients do not respond at all, many suffer emotional numbing and loss of libido that sometimes never returns, and withdrawal can be severe enough to trap patients on the drugs.
insights.speaker: Andrew Scull
insights.so_what: The most prescribed antidepressant class delivers modest average benefit with a large non-responder tail and a dependency dynamic, which is the central vulnerability for both litigation and displacement by alternatives.
insights.quote: for most patients, antidepressants are marginally better than placebo, but a lot of the effect is the placebo effect

insights.claim: FDA approval required only two positive trials regardless of how many failed, so a sponsor could run fifteen trials with thirteen failures and still win approval, while drug companies funded the studies, owned the data and released only what helped them.
insights.speaker: Andrew Scull
insights.so_what: The approval standard itself institutionalizes publication bias, so the apparent efficacy of any approved psychiatric drug is an upper bound rather than an estimate.
insights.quote: You might have conducted 15 trials and 13 of them had been failures, but if you had two that worked, that was enough.

themes.theme: Hype, trust and the research pipeline

insights.claim: Scull says ketamine and psychedelics are currently being propounded as a miracle cure for depression on evidence that is enormously weak, and explicitly places this in the same pattern as the repeated 80 percent cure claims of the asylum, insulin coma and focal sepsis eras.
insights.speaker: Andrew Scull
insights.so_what: A direct against-consensus call on the psychedelic therapeutics cycle from the historian who has catalogued every prior psychiatric enthusiasm that collapsed.
insights.quote: Ketamine and psychedelics being propounded as a miracle cure for depression, and the evidence for that is enormously weak

insights.claim: Scull locates the hype problem not only in science journalism but inside the gatekeeping journals, arguing Science and Nature foreground findings that make a big splash while negative findings, which are what prevent mistakes, do not get published.
insights.speaker: Andrew Scull
insights.so_what: The selection filter for breakthrough claims runs through the journals themselves, so discounting hype requires discounting the primary literature and not just its press coverage.
insights.quote: negative findings are very important in science

insights.claim: Scull argues current US research funding cuts are destroying science in ways that are invisible because they are counterfactual: clinical trials aborted midway lose that knowledge permanently, scientists are not being trained, and since it takes at least six or seven years to train a scientist, four years of cuts costs roughly a decade.
insights.speaker: Andrew Scull
insights.so_what: The damage compounds on a multi-year lag and shows up as an absence of future discoveries rather than as a visible event, so the cost will not appear in any near-term data series.
insights.quote: it takes at least six or seven years to train a scientist at the beginning of their career

insights.claim: Scull treats institutional trust as an asset that is slow to build and fast to destroy, warning that vaccination distrust is generalizing into broad distrust of science and medicine and that mistrust will grow exponentially over four years.
insights.speaker: Andrew Scull
insights.so_what: Erosion of trust is a structural headwind for every evidence-dependent health business, independent of whether any particular product works.
insights.quote: once trust is lost, it's very hard to recover

insights.claim: US public policy abandoned the seriously mentally ill by closing asylums in favor of a community care that never materialized, so the three largest centers of inpatient psychiatric care are now the Los Angeles County Jail, Cook County Jail and Rikers Island, and people with serious mental illness die fifteen to twenty-five years early with that gap widening.
insights.speaker: Andrew Scull
insights.so_what: The real cost of deinstitutionalization was transferred to jails and to mortality, which is where any honest cost-benefit case for rebuilding psychiatric capacity has to start.
insights.quote: Community care is a shell game without a pee.

insights.claim: Scull's prescription is to broaden psychiatric research beyond drugs, neuroscience and genetics into psychosocial dimensions and to make careers viable there, noting that academic psychiatrists depend entirely on grants and there is no grant money to study better ways of handling homelessness or of supporting families living with a hallucinating relative.
insights.speaker: Andrew Scull
insights.so_what: The funding structure, not clinical need, determines which questions get asked, so an entire category of cheaper interventions goes untested for want of a grant line.
